claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in fusion plasma-facing structural materials is primarily governed by grain-boundary stability and mobility.
High-temperature toughness in fusion plasma-facing structural materials is primarily governed by grain-boundary stability and mobility.
The relevant grain-boundary property is the propensity for sliding and migration under thermal and irradiation conditions.
Thermomechanical processing can produce samples enriched in low-angle or special boundaries while grain size and composition are held constant.
At high temperatures, grain-boundary sliding accommodates plastic strain.
At high temperatures, grain-boundary migration accommodates plastic strain.
Random high-angle grain boundaries have higher mobility than low-angle or special grain boundaries.
The higher mobility of random high-angle boundaries facilitates plasticity.
Random high-angle boundaries can serve as sites for void nucleation.
Random high-angle boundaries can serve as paths or sites for crack propagation.
Void nucleation and crack propagation at mobile grain boundaries reduce toughness.
Increasing the fraction of low-mobility boundaries suppresses grain-boundary sliding.
Suppressing grain-boundary sliding reduces high-temperature plastic strain.
Increasing the fraction of low-angle or special boundaries will increase toughness relative to a random-high-angle-boundary baseline.
The proposed effects apply to micron-grained polycrystalline metallic alloys above 0.5 Tm when severe grain growth and amorphization are absent.
Dislocation climb and precipitation may also contribute to high-temperature deformation and toughness.
